passages.t: Bold after Philippi, and not out for money or praise
passages.happening:
“You yourselves know, brothers, that our visit to you was not in vain” (verse 1). Paul reminds them what had happened just before: “we had already endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi. But in the face of strong opposition, we were bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God” (verse 2).

Then he says what kind of messengers they were. “For our appeal does not arise from deceit or ulterior motives or trickery. Instead, we speak as those approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, not in order to please men but God, who examines our hearts” (verses 3-4). They never used flattery, never had greed behind their words, and never looked for praise, though as apostles they could have demanded it (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
The Thessalonians knew what Paul meant by Philippi. Acts tells how he and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into prison there, with their feet fastened in the stocks (Acts 16:22-24). Roman citizens were not supposed to be treated that way, and it was a public shame. Then they walked on to Thessalonica and started preaching again, in the face of more opposition. That is what Paul means by ‘bold in our God’. The courage was not theirs. It came from God.

Why does Paul spend so long saying what they were not? Greek cities were full of travelling speakers and teachers. Some were serious. Many were not. They went from town to town giving speeches, gathering followers, taking fees or finding a rich patron, and moving on. People knew the type, and critics said such men were flatterers, greedy and vain. Paul had left Thessalonica suddenly, by night. To his neighbours' eyes that could look like one more charlatan's exit. Scholars do not agree whether someone was actually accusing Paul, or whether he simply draws the contrast. Either way, he asks the church to remember what they saw with their own eyes.

Notice the phrase ‘God, who examines our hearts’. The word means to test, the way metal is tested to show whether it is real. Paul says his motives have been tested by the only one who can see them. He is not trying to please the crowd. And ‘God is our witness’ is a solemn oath. He means it.
passages.ot:
The prophets also spoke boldly in the face of threats. God told Jeremiah, “Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you” (Jeremiah 1:8). Jeremiah found he could not keep quiet: “His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9).

That God tests the heart is a steady theme of the Old Testament. “I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind” (Jeremiah 17:10). When Samuel looked at the outside of a man, God told him, “the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

Proverbs warns about the very things Paul refused. “The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high” (Proverbs 29:25). And “a flattering mouth causes ruin” (Proverbs 26:28).
passages.asks: Paul asks the Thessalonians to judge him by how he lived, not by what others said. Ask whose approval you most want, and how much it shapes what you say. Ask where flattery has crept into your words, at work, at church or at home. And if you lead or teach others in any way, ask whether you could say, as Paul did, that God is your witness.

passages.t: Gentle as a nursing mother, caring as a father
passages.happening:
“On the contrary, we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her children. We cared so deeply that we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well. That is how beloved you have become to us” (verses 7-8).

“Surely you recall, brothers, our labor and toil. We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God” (verse 9). They lived holy, upright and blameless lives among them (verse 10).

“For you know that we treated each of you as a father treats his own children— encouraging you, comforting you, and urging you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
Paul could have stood on his rights as an apostle. Instead he reaches for two pictures from family life.

The first is a nursing mother. The Greek word could mean a hired nurse, but ‘her children’ shows that Paul means a mother feeding and warming her own baby. It is a picture of tender, patient, costly care. It is a striking picture for a man to use of himself, and Paul chose it.

There is a small puzzle in verse 7. Many early Greek copies read ‘we were infants among you’, while others read ‘we were gentle among you’. In Greek the two words differ by one letter. The BSB has ‘gentle’, which fits the nursing mother smoothly; the copies that say ‘infants’ are many and early. Scholars are divided. Either way the point is the same: Paul did not throw his weight around.

Then Paul says they shared ‘not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well’. They did not hand over a message and leave. They lived among the people they taught.

They also worked. Acts says Paul's trade was making tents (Acts 18:3), work with leather or cloth. In that world the upper classes looked down on work with the hands, and a teacher who did it would be noticed. Paul did it so that no one could say he was in it for the money, and so that the poor in the church would not have to carry him.

The second picture is a father. In that world a father was responsible for teaching his children how to live. Paul says he did that ‘each of you’, one by one, with encouragement, comfort and urging. A good father's care is personal, and it has a goal: that his children grow up to walk ‘in a manner worthy of God’.
passages.ot:
God himself is pictured as a mother. “As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13). “Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb? Even if she could forget, I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15).

Moses, worn out by the people, complained to God, “Did I give them birth, so that You should tell me, ‘Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries an infant,’” (Numbers 11:12). Paul takes up that very picture, and gladly.

And God is pictured as a father. “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him” (Psalm 103:13). In the wilderness, Moses said, “the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son” (Deuteronomy 1:31).
passages.hard:
Paul pictures himself as a father who encourages, comforts and urges. What if ‘father’ is a hard word for you? Some readers had a father who was absent, or who hurt them.

Paul is describing what a father in the faith should be: someone who knows each child, encourages, comforts and patiently guides. If your own father was not that, this is a picture of what you should have been shown. A psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). If what happened to you still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And if you lead others, whether in a church, a home or a job, Paul's two pictures are a test. A leader who frightens, controls or uses people is not acting as a mother or a father in Paul's sense at all.
passages.asks: Paul gave not only the message but his own life. Ask whom you are sharing your life with, not only your opinions. Ask whether there is anyone you could encourage, comfort or patiently guide this week, as a good mother or father would. And ask whether you have ever let anyone carry a burden you could have carried yourself.

passages.t: The word of God at work, and suffering for it
passages.happening:
Paul gives thanks again. “And we continually thank God because, when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as the true word of God—the word which is now at work in you who believe” (verse 13).

Then he speaks of their suffering. “For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Judea that are in Christ Jesus. You suffered from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews” (verse 14). He goes on to speak sharply of those in Judea who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, drove out the missionaries, and hindered them from speaking to the Gentiles ‘how they may be saved’ (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
Verse 13 says something remarkable. The Thessalonians heard human voices, Paul's and Silas's and Timothy's. But what they heard was God speaking. And that word did not just inform them. It is ‘at work’ in them, still doing things, changing them from the inside.

Then Paul puts their suffering in a larger story. The Thessalonians were Gentiles, and the people making life hard for them were their own Gentile neighbours: ‘your own countrymen’. The first churches, in Judea, were made up of Jews, and the people who made life hard for them were some of their own Jewish neighbours. Paul knew that story from the inside. Before he met Christ, he had been one of those who hunted the believers in Judea (Galatians 1:13).

So when the Thessalonians suffered, they were not strange or alone. They were walking where the Judean believers had walked, and where Jesus and the prophets had walked before them.

Verses 15 and 16 are some of the hardest words in Paul's letters, and they need great care. The part below faces them.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament itself tells, with sorrow, how God's messengers were rejected by their own people. Elijah said, “the Israelites have forsaken Your covenant, torn down Your altars, and killed Your prophets with the sword” (1 Kings 19:10). Jeremiah was threatened by the men of his own home town (Jeremiah 11:21), and King Jehoiakim had the prophet Uriah put to the sword (Jeremiah 26:23). Chronicles sums it up: “Again and again the LORD, the God of their fathers, sent word to His people through His messengers because He had compassion on them” (2 Chronicles 36:15).

These are Israel's own Scriptures, written by Israel's own prophets about their own people. Paul's sharp words stand in that line: a voice from inside the family, not an attack from outside it.

And God's word at work is like the word in Jeremiah: “Is not My word like fire,” declares the LORD, “and like a hammer that smashes a rock?” (Jeremiah 23:29).
passages.hard:
Verses 14 to 16 say that some in Judea killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, opposed the mission, and face God's wrath. Are these words against the Jewish people?

No. These verses have been badly misused, so they must be read with the greatest care.

First, see who is speaking. Paul is a Jew, writing as a Jew. Jesus was a Jew. So were the apostles, and so were all the believers in the churches of Judea that Paul is speaking of. They suffered too.

Second, see whom he means. Paul is speaking of particular people in particular places: those in Judea who opposed the gospel, drove out its messengers and tried to stop it reaching the Gentiles. He sets them beside the Thessalonians' own Gentile neighbours, who were doing the same in Thessalonica. The Judean churches suffered from their own countrymen; the Thessalonians suffered from theirs. Paul compares persecutors with persecutors, not one people with another. And his words sound like Israel's own prophets, who spoke just as sharply about those of their own people who rejected God's messengers.

Third, hear the same Paul elsewhere. Of his own people he writes, “For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood” (Romans 9:3). And he asks, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1).

What Paul meant by ‘the utmost wrath has come upon them’ (verse 16) is debated; scholars have suggested several things he may have had in view. A few have argued that verses 15 and 16 were added by a later hand, but no manuscript lacks them, and most accept them as Paul's. On any reading, these verses are not a verdict on the Jewish people, then or now.

For centuries some Christians used words like these to call Jews ‘Christ-killers’, to teach contempt for them, and to justify cruelty and violence against them. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. As that note says, the New Testament places all people inside the guilt for the death of Jesus, Gentile and Jew alike.
passages.asks: Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians heard God's own word through human voices. Ask how you receive the word of God: as one more opinion, or as God speaking to you. Ask whether anyone has made your life hard for your faith, and whether you can see that you are not alone. And ask whether you have ever been the one who made it hard for someone else.

passages.t: Torn away, and longing to return
passages.happening:
“Brothers, although we were torn away from you for a short time (in person, not in heart), our desire to see you face to face was even more intense” (verse 17). “For we wanted to come to you—indeed I, Paul, tried again and again—but Satan obstructed us” (verse 18).

“After all, who is our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting, if it is not you yourselves in the presence of our Lord Jesus at His coming? You are indeed our glory and our joy” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
The word Paul uses for ‘torn away’ was used of a child who had lost its parents. It means to be orphaned. Paul has just called himself their mother and their father. Now he says that when he was taken from them, he felt like a child who had lost his family. The love ran both ways.

Here for the first time in the letter Paul speaks alone: ‘I, Paul’. He wants them to know that he did not forget them. He tried to come back ‘again and again’.

‘Satan obstructed us.’ Paul does not say how. He does not blame the Thessalonians, or God, or himself. He names an enemy who opposes the work of the gospel. But notice what he does next. He does not give up. In the next chapter he sends Timothy instead.

Then Paul looks ahead to ‘the coming’ of the Lord Jesus. The Greek word, parousia, was used when a ruler arrived on an official visit, with crowds and ceremony. This is the first time the letter uses it for Jesus. When that day comes, Paul pictures himself standing before the Lord with the Thessalonians, and they will be his ‘crown of boasting’. A crown in that world was often a wreath given to a winner. Paul's prize will not be anything he gained for himself. It will be the people he loved.
passages.ot:
The prophets pictured God's people as a crown in God's own hand. “You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God” (Isaiah 62:3). And Proverbs says that family is a crown: “Grandchildren are the crown of the aged” (Proverbs 17:6). Paul, the spiritual father, says his children in the faith are his.

Scripture also speaks of a power that opposes God's servants. Zechariah saw “Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him”, and heard “The LORD rebukes you, Satan!” (Zechariah 3:1-2). Daniel was told that his prayer was heard from the first day, though ‘the prince of the kingdom of Persia’ opposed the messenger for twenty-one days (Daniel 10:12-13). Opposition is real. God is greater.
passages.asks: Paul calls the Thessalonians his glory and joy. Ask who your joy is, and whether they know it. Ask what you hope to have in your hands on the day the Lord comes: things, or people you have loved. And if something has kept you from doing good you meant to do, ask what other way might still be open, as Paul found when he sent Timothy.
